subject: Anthropology
title: Stratigraphy
description: A micro-lesson that makes Stratigraphy usable.

hook.text: Dig straight down and you travel backward in time. The deepest layer is the oldest. Dirt keeps a calendar.

buildup.text: Stratigraphy is the study of soil layers. Each layer represents a period of human activity or natural deposition.

discovery.text: The law of superposition says lower layers are older than upper ones, giving archaeologists a relative timeline.

twist.text: Disturbances like plowing, burrowing animals, or later construction can mix layers, complicating the record.

climax.text: Stratigraphy turns dirt into a timeline. Reading layers carefully is the foundation of all excavation work.

punchline.text: Every layer of soil is a page of history.

quiz.question: What does the law of superposition state?
options: Lower layers are older than upper ones
All layers are the same age

details.summary: Stratigraphy is the study of soil layers deposited over time at archaeological sites. Older layers lie beneath newer ones, creating a chronological sequence. By reading these layers, archaeologists establish relative dating and reconstruct the history of human activity at a site.
details.whyItMatters: Stratigraphy provides the fundamental framework for ordering the past. Before absolute dating methods existed, reading soil layers was the primary way to determine what happened before what at any given site.
takeaways: Older deposits lie beneath newer ones in undisturbed sites
Soil layers create a chronological sequence of past activity
Stratigraphy is the foundation for relative dating in archaeology

faq.question: Can stratigraphy be disrupted or misleading?
faq.answer: Yes. Animal burrows, tree roots, later construction, and human digging can mix layers. Erosion can remove layers entirely. Archaeologists must identify these disturbances to avoid misinterpreting the chronological sequence. Careful excavation is essential.

faq.question: How does stratigraphy relate to absolute dating?
faq.answer: Stratigraphy tells you what is older or newer relative to other layers. Absolute dating methods like radiocarbon dating assign actual calendar dates. Combining both gives the most complete chronological picture of a site's history.
